llm.summary: The AI complex is bouncing: chip names (MU, AMD, Nvidia, Broadcom) rebound, CoreWeave jumps on a Goldman upgrade, and Applied Digital/TeraWulf/IREN rise 6-8% as Nasdaq futures lead. But the bounce sits on the same cracked foundation as Friday — The Information and The Decoder both flag a 'neocloud shakeout', Nscale's IPO is getting valuation pushback, and Microsoft abandoned a UK AI supercomputer because the grid can't feed it. The relief is rate-driven: oil fell on Trump's Russian sanctions waiver, that pulled yields down and December hike odds with it, lifting gold-adjacent and long-duration risk simultaneously. That is a fragile mechanism — the same waiver that eased crude can be reversed, and Bessent is already framing September's 3.7% CPI as an 'energy shock', which cuts both ways. Structurally the news keeps confirming the thesis that electrons and capital, not chips, are the binding constraint: gas plant construction costs +66%, Japanese power prices +25%, India demand +11%, Duke guiding 2026 profit higher, pipeline owners racing to add capacity. The second leg is Nvidia's expanding moat into physical AI (Siemens autonomous factories, Reply's Physical AI specialization, Santander) just as Amazon attacks its software moat by making Trainium work with Triton/CUDA-adjacent tooling — the first credible assault on the switching-cost layer. Defense stocks tumbled on a Democratic sweep bet even as JPMorgan committed $5bn to robot factories and hypersonics, a clean divergence between political tape and industrial reality. Today's risk calendar: Netflix prints tomorrow with the stock already down 23%, Meta/Tesla later in a 70-company week, and GE/FITB/STLD report this morning into a market where Financials (-45) and Industrials (-50) rotation is deeply negative.

market_thesis.short_term: Days-to-weeks: this is a dead-cat-with-a-catalyst bounce, not a resolution. Yields eased only because oil fell on a discretionary sanctions waiver — a policy, not a fundamental, and Reuters is already asking 'wavering waiver?'. Equity upside is being rented from the rates market. The dispersion trade remains the right expression: long the AI income statement (Nvidia's physical-AI partnerships, Micron/memory, on-device inference, agentic software with real cash flow) and short the AI balance sheet (neoclouds, Nscale's IPO, leveraged compute intermediaries, data-centre paper). CoreWeave rallying on a sell-side upgrade while the same week's reporting calls a shakeout is exactly the kind of sentiment-versus-structure gap that resolves against sentiment. Netflix tomorrow and Meta/Tesla later are the week's volatility nodes; with Communication Services flows deteriorating and the sector at -32 rotation, the market is positioned to punish any ad or capex disappointment.
market_thesis.medium_term: Months: the regime print — Reflation 28.3 (+11.4) and Stagflation 26.1 (+7.6) against Goldilocks 23.7 (-7.1) — says the inflation distribution keeps fattening at both ends while the benign middle drains. The AI buildout is itself now a named inflation input (Yardeni, Fed commentary), which means the Fed cannot ease into the capex cycle the way equity bulls need. Power is the cleanest expression of that: gas plant capex +66%, Japanese retail electricity +25%, European demand reviving on data centres and electrification. Whoever owns ratebase, pipelines, turbines or uprated nuclear gets paid regardless of which model or neocloud wins. Simultaneously the fiscal leg is hardening — a $1.99tn deficit with interest expense exceeding defense spending, France's debt crisis dragging the euro and Paris-listed assets — which caps how far long yields can fall and keeps a structural bid under gold even when it stalls below $4,200. The consumer stays bifurcated: 440,000 new US millionaires in 2025 on asset prices, against cash making a comeback in India and electricity-bill-assistance queries rising here.
market_thesis.long_term: Years: three structural moves are visible in today's tape. First, the compute moat is migrating from silicon to software-plus-power; Amazon making its own chips speak the popular coding language is the opening salvo in commoditising CUDA, and even a partial success compresses the terminal margin assumption embedded in the entire semiconductor complex. Second, AI is leaving the data centre — Siemens autonomous factories, Reply's physical AI/digital twins, agents running locally on 128GB laptops — which decouples adoption from hyperscaler capex and re-rates the edge device, industrial automation and sensing supply chain. Third, electricity becomes the scarce consumer and industrial good of the decade; Microsoft abandoning a UK supercomputer over grid capacity is the canonical datapoint that siting follows electrons, not talent or tax. Underneath, the household is being repriced from an asset economy to an income economy — gasoline-led CPI, surging utility bills, a frozen housing transaction market with 'housing market crash' searches up 32% — which permanently favours affordability, essential health, regulated power and sellers of cost removal to businesses over sellers of aspiration to consumers.

short_term: Households are rationing around energy: 'electricity bill assistance' and 'electricity bill calculator' are top rising queries while Japanese power prices jump 25% — utilities are shifting from a background bill to an actively managed budget line.

Retail investors are chasing the bounce rather than the structure — buying Monday 'despite fear the AI trade nightmare scenario is far from over' — which means positioning is thin-conviction and reverses fast on a single bad print.

Income hunger is overwhelming risk discipline: boomers piling into options-income ETFs without understanding the tax treatment, dividend-yield screens dominating retail headlines, and a flood of unsolicited $15,000 loan offers at 8%.

Enterprises are shifting AI spend from experimentation to cost-per-token: Nvidia-backed doubleAI launching a model to pare compute cost, Datadog punished for an AI customer cutting usage — buyers are now optimising, not just expanding.

Attention is concentrating on housing and space as personal, not financial, topics — Starlink queries up 49% (connectivity as mobility/autonomy), housing-crash queries up 32% (security) — both flagged not-priced.

Savers and merchants are hedging digital fragility: cash is 'making a comeback' in digital India, China accelerating gold accumulation, Dubai-China gold trade MoU — a quiet preference for settlement you can hold.
long_term: Compute moves to where power is, not where people are — Microsoft's abandoned UK supercomputer makes grid interconnection the primary siting variable for a decade of industrial investment.

Work gets re-bundled around agents: single-core CPU performance mattering again, 74B-class models on laptops, and factories that self-configure via digital twins — the unit of labour becomes supervision of autonomous systems rather than execution.

The education-to-employment pipeline is already repricing — colleges that raced to build computer-science departments now face a bust, the first visible labour-market scar from AI-driven productivity.

Energy becomes a status and security good, not a utility: households with on-site generation, backup and favourable tariffs will be structurally advantaged, mirroring how water access worked in prior scarcity regimes.

Sovereigns treat compute, enrichment, rare earths and index inclusion as instruments of statecraft — China's export curbs on machinery to India, Nvidia's CEO pleading for US-China cooperation, and gold accumulation all point to a world where supply chains are chosen politically, not economically.

Fiscal arithmetic becomes a household-level concern as interest expense exceeds defense spending; expect persistent demand for inflation-protected income, hard assets and non-sovereign stores of value even when crypto itself disappoints.

But Datadog's 19% fall on an AI customer cutting usage is the warning: consumption-based AI revenue is not yet durable. Hold at 5%, do not add until a clean seat-plus-consumption print.
